M from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; density 1.544 g/mL at 25 C and aqueous solubility 90.9 g/100 mL water at 25 C: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. Solid molar heat capacity 236.6 J/(mol.K) is an explicit editorial estimate by Kopp's rule from the additive contributions C 10.89, H 7.56, O 13.42 J/(mol.K), not a measurement. The substance modelled is D-glucose in its pyranose ring form, and the physical properties above are D-glucose's. The curated SMILES and official-library InChIKey carry the D configuration while deliberately leaving the anomeric centre unspecified, so identity distinguishes D- from L-glucose without pretending to choose the alpha or beta anomer. The key is not asserted; it is what the official IUPAC library computes. Enthalpy of solution is not claimed

NO INCHIKEY IS ASSERTED: writing one means choosing a stereochemistry, and fermentation lactic acid is a mixture of the L-(+) and D-(-) forms in proportions that depend on which organism made it, so this record claims neither. Aqueous solubility is not entered because the acid is miscible with water in all proportions and a finite g/100 mL would be a false ceiling. ACIDITY IS NOT MODELLED: none of the three databases this lab loads defines a lactate species - wateq4f, minteq.v4 and pitzer were searched by name, and the only vendored file that carries Lactate is llnl-organics, which is not among them - so this acid enters solution as a finite neutral solute and its carboxylic proton is absent from any computed pH. The engine says so out loud rather than reporting a silently neutral solution. Enthalpy of solution is not claimed

Brochantite, antlerite and langite — the basic copper sulfates that wateq4f and minteq.v4 report a cooling copper sulfate solution as supersaturated against. Added so the aqueous engine has something to precipitate rather than only a sentence to say, exactly as atacamite was. Formulae and molar masses from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; densities and colours are standard mineralogical values; molar heat capacities are Kopp's-rule estimates and explicit teaching approximations. No thermodynamic constant is asserted here: each phase is defined by the shipped database and matched to its species by composition — which is why langite is written here as the MONOhydrate Cu4SO4(OH)6.H2O. Mineralogical langite is the dihydrate; wateq4f defines the phase with one water, and the match is on exact composition INCLUDING waters of crystallisation, so a dihydrate entry would never have met the phase it was added for. The registry follows the database it has to match and records the discrepancy rather than hiding it

Formulae and molar masses from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; densities and colours are standard mineralogical values; molar heat capacities are Kopp's-rule estimates and explicit teaching approximations. No thermodynamic constant is asserted here: each phase is defined by the shipped database and matched to its species by composition — which is why langite is written here as the MONOhydrate Cu4SO4(OH)6.H2O. Mineralogical langite is the dihydrate; wateq4f defines the phase with one water, and the match is on exact composition INCLUDING waters of crystallisation, so a dihydrate entry would never have met the phase it was added for. The registry follows the database it has to match and records the discrepancy rather than hiding it

ammonium nitrate: the cold-pack salt: dissolving it is strongly endothermic, which is the whole of an instant cold pack. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; density and appearance are standard reference values; the molar heat capacity is a Kopp's-rule estimate and an explicit teaching approximation. The enthalpy of dissolution, +25.7 kJ/mol, is the number the cold pack is for: one of the most strongly endothermic dissolutions a kitchen can produce, and the reason the pack goes cold rather than merely failing to warm.

graphite: the layered allotrope of carbon — soft, opaque, and the one in a pencil. Separate from the registry's charcoal carbon and from diamond because the point of comparing them is that one element gives three different solids. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; density and appearance are standard reference values; the molar heat capacity is a Kopp's-rule estimate and an explicit teaching approximation.

diamond: the tetrahedral allotrope: the same carbon atoms as graphite, 55% denser, and transparent instead of black. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; density and appearance are standard reference values; the molar heat capacity is a Kopp's-rule estimate and an explicit teaching approximation. The bench has no transparency for a solid, so diamond is described as white rather than clear — the one property a person would name first is the one this appearance model cannot express. That is stated here because a reader who sees 'white diamond' should know it is a limit of the description and not a claim about the stone.

methane, the simplest alkane and the main component of natural gas. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 35.7 J/(mol.K) at 298 K: standard reference values. The NASA CEA record this species matches by composition is what makes it burn; density is the bench's shared gas placeholder of 1.0 g/mL, the same figure O2, N2, H2 and CO2 carry: a gas is added by the mole and its volume comes from the vessel's headspace, so no run reads this number. Odour is not modelled: the smell of a gas leak is the added odorant, not the methane.

propane, the bottled-gas alkane. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 73.6 J/(mol.K) at 298 K: standard reference values. It is entered as the gas because that is the phase it burns in; the liquid under pressure inside the bottle is a state this bench does not hold, so nothing here describes a cylinder. density is the bench's shared gas placeholder of 1.0 g/mL, the same figure O2, N2, H2 and CO2 carry: a gas is added by the mole and its volume comes from the vessel's headspace, so no run reads this number.

butane, the lighter-fuel alkane, as n-butane. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 98.5 J/(mol.K) at 298 K for n-butane: standard reference values. Isobutane has the same formula and is a different substance with its own boiling point; this record is the straight chain and does not distinguish the two, so a composition match may reach either isomer's thermochemistry. density is the bench's shared gas placeholder of 1.0 g/mL, the same figure O2, N2, H2 and CO2 carry: a gas is added by the mole and its volume comes from the vessel's headspace, so no run reads this number.

helium, the monatomic noble gas. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 20.8 J/(mol.K) is 5R/2, exact for an ideal monatomic gas and the reason helium's heat capacity is the same at every temperature a bench reaches. Chemically it does nothing at all, which is the point of having it: whatever pressure it makes in a sealed vessel is the pressure the amount of substance makes, with no chemistry underneath. density is the bench's shared gas placeholder of 1.0 g/mL, the same figure O2, N2, H2 and CO2 carry: a gas is added by the mole and its volume comes from the vessel's headspace, so no run reads this number.

naphthalene, the fused two-ring aromatic sold as mothballs. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; density 1.14 g/mL and Cp(s) 165.7 J/(mol.K) at 298 K: standard reference values. The aqueous solubility of 0.003 g/100 mL is the reviewed room-temperature figure and is entered so the bench can say it does not dissolve rather than apologise for not knowing. Appearance is recorded as white; the smell, which is the property a person would name first, is not modelled at all.

hydrogen sulfide, the gas that tarnishes silver and that a rotten egg smells of. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 34.2 J/(mol.K) at 298 K: standard reference values. It is recorded as colourless because it is; the smell is the property that matters most about it in a room and this bench has no odour entry for it, so nothing in a run will warn a reader by nose. No sulfide solution chemistry is installed either: there is no S(-2) species on the shelf, so this gas dissolves into nothing and forms no metal sulfide. density is the bench's shared gas placeholder of 1.0 g/mL, the same figure O2, N2, H2 and CO2 carry: a gas is added by the mole and its volume comes from the vessel's headspace, so no run reads this number.

chlorophyll a, the magnesium porphyrin that makes a leaf green. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over the accepted C55H72MgN4O5 formula; density 1.079 g/mL is a standard reference value and the molar heat capacity is a Kopp's-rule estimate and an explicit teaching approximation. No InChIKey is asserted: this record stands for the chlorophyll of a leaf, and chlorophyll b and the several allomers a real extract contains are not distinguished. The colour is RECORDED, not computed: chlorophyll looks green because it absorbs strongly in the blue near 430 nm and in the red near 665 nm and reflects what is left, and this species carries no absorption spectrum, so nothing in a run derives the green from those two bands. Photosynthesis is not modelled anywhere on this bench, so holding the pigment is not holding the process.

nylon 6,6 as one adipamide repeat unit, the same polymer-as-population convention polyethylene and PET already use. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over the repeat unit; density 1.14 g/mL is a standard reference value and the molar heat capacity is a Kopp's-rule estimate and an explicit teaching approximation. No InChIKey is asserted, because a chain of indefinite length is not a molecule. NO aqueous solubility is entered either, and that is deliberate: the other polymers on this shelf carry a reviewed zero so the bench can say they do not dissolve, but nylon IS attacked by hot concentrated acid - the amide bond hydrolyses - and no solver here models that. Entering a zero would turn a gap into the claim that the polymer survives, so this record stays silent and the engine says it does not know.

M from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(s) and density are the standard reference room-temperature values for alpha-uranium. This entry exists so the bench can answer whether a block of uranium warms itself through its own decay (curiosity corpus th-122), and it is a metal on a ledger rather than a metal on a shelf: no acquisition, handling, storage or disposal claim is made or implied by its presence here. The block is modelled as pure U-238; natural uranium's specific activity is about twice this, because U-234 at roughly 54 ppm sits in secular equilibrium with U-238 and contributes almost as many decays again, and the 0.72% U-235 adds a little more. The L0 safety screen has no radiological class, so uranium is filed there by its chemistry alone - it is an active metal and displaces hydrogen from acid - which is wrong about the world in the same way the lead row already says it is, and is written down rather than hidden

carbon monoxide, the product a flame makes when it runs short of air. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 29.1 J/(mol.K) at 298 K: standard reference values. It is here because two engines already named it and neither could weigh it: the gas mechanism packs deposit CO by name, and NASA CEA's equilibrium product pool is exactly the set this registry can name - so a rich flame had no carbon monoxide to make and dissociation above about 2000 K had nowhere to go. Adding the word is therefore a physics change and not only a vocabulary one, and the flames in this repository move because of it. density is the bench's shared gas placeholder of 1.0 g/mL, the same figure O2, N2, H2 and CO2 carry: a gas is added by the mole and its volume comes from the vessel's headspace, so no run reads this number. What is NOT claimed here is the hazard a person meets: carbon monoxide is odourless and binds haemoglobin some two hundred times more tightly than oxygen does, and this bench has no odour entry for it, no inhalation model, and no safety group for a sparingly soluble acutely toxic gas

n-dodecane, the light half of this bench's diesel surrogate and the n-alkane most often used as one in the combustion literature. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(l) 375.8 J/(mol.K) at 298 K and density 0.7495 g/mL at 20 C are the commonly tabulated handbook values, PENDING REVIEW: no positively identified copy of a handbook edition was opened for this row, so no edition-level provenance is claimed. NASA CEA's thermo.inp carries no C12 alkane at all - its saturated chain records stop at n-octane and the n-decyl radical - so this species never reaches the equilibrium flame solver, and `ignite` answers it through the curated combustion table instead, which states its own heat of combustion and its own autoignition temperature

n-hexadecane - cetane - the heavy half of this bench's diesel surrogate and the substance the cetane number is defined against: it is cetane number 100 by definition, which is why a diesel surrogate is built around it rather than around any other C16. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(l) 501.6 J/(mol.K) at 298 K and density 0.77 g/mL at 20 C are the commonly tabulated handbook values, PENDING REVIEW: no positively identified copy of a handbook edition was opened for this row, so no edition-level provenance is claimed. Note the melting point: cetane freezes at 18 C, a few degrees below room temperature, which is the real reason winter diesel is a different blend from summer diesel - the bench holds the number but models no wax precipitation and no cold filter plugging. NASA CEA's thermo.inp carries no C16 alkane, so this species burns through the curated combustion table rather than the equilibrium flame solver

A melanin surrogate, and deliberately not melanin. Eumelanin is a heterogeneous cross-linked biopolymer with no molecular formula and no molar mass, so this row stands for ONE 5,6-dihydroxyindole repeat unit, C8H7NO2 - the accepted building block of it - using the same polymer-as-population convention polyethylene, PET and nylon already use on this shelf. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over that repeat unit. The molar heat capacity, 179.5 J/(mol.K), is a Kopp's-rule estimate over the atomic contributions C 10.89, H 7.56, N 12.66 and O 13.42, and is an explicit teaching approximation. The density, 1.6 g/mL, is the figure commonly quoted for melanin granules and IS PENDING REVIEW: no positively identified source is claimed for it, and it is flagged for reviewer confirmation. No InChIKey is asserted, because a pigment of indefinite length and irregular linkage is not a molecule; eumelanin, pheomelanin and the carboxylated DHICA units a real hair contains are not distinguished, and neither are the red-blond pigments. THE COLOUR IS RECORDED, NOT COMPUTED: this species carries no absorption spectrum, so melanin's characteristic featureless absorbance rising monotonically towards the blue is nowhere in this record, and a run has only a reflective value on a solid. Nothing here models a hair fibre, a cuticle, a melanosome, or the diffusion of anything into one - the pigment is a powder in a beaker. A REVIEWED AQUEOUS SOLUBILITY OF ZERO is entered deliberately, on the precedent the polymers on this shelf set: melanin is insoluble in water, and recording the zero is what lets the bench say so instead of apologising for not knowing. Note what that sentence then does NOT know about: the honesty pass that speaks it asks the curated reaction table whether anything is consuming the solid, and does not yet ask the kinetic network, so while the bleach is running the bench prints a true remark about dissolution beside it in words that read as though the pigment were untouched. That is a gap in that pass, it is recorded here where a reader meets it, and it is not fixed by this record.

The colourless product of oxidising the pigment above, and a BOOKKEEPING SPECIES rather than an identified compound. Peroxide bleaching really cleaves the melanin chromophore into a mixture of smaller, largely carboxylic fragments, and no single one of them is this row. What the row does is conserve the atoms and stop absorbing light, which is the same convention the hypochlorite decolourisations on this shelf already use for indigo carmine, betanin and curcumin: the parent formula plus exactly one oxygen. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over C8H7NO3; the molar heat capacity, 192.9 J/(mol.K), is the parent's Kopp's-rule estimate plus one oxygen contribution, and the density is carried over from the parent unchanged. Both are explicit teaching approximations and the density is PENDING REVIEW with the parent's. No InChIKey is asserted, because no single molecule is meant. It is colourless because it carries no absorption spectrum and an off-white reflective value - a RECORDED absence, not a computed one. A reviewed aqueous solubility of zero is entered for the same reason as the parent's, and carries the same caveat about the honesty pass.

Kerotakis curated phase-transition tranche v1: normal melting, boiling, sublimation, decomposition and hydrate-dehydration temperatures at 101.325 kPa. Each value is an individually entered editorial constant, taken from the standard published values for these substances and cross-checked against general reference tables. It is NOT a transcription from a positively identified copy of any single handbook edition, and no edition-level provenance is claimed: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. is the intended primary reference and every value here is flagged for reviewer confirmation against a positively identified copy of it before any stronger claim is made. (Reviewer confirmation recorded 2026-09-01 in the registry source's own citation; this seed constant is historical - the bootstrap only fires when the source record is absent.) Values are recorded only to the precision a school apparatus resolves; where a substance decomposes or sublimes rather than melting, no melting point is claimed at all; and where two general references disagreed the value was dropped rather than averaged or guessed. Compiled 2026-08-29

Kerotakis curated dissolution-enthalpy tranche v1: molar enthalpy of dissolution in water at 298.15 K and infinite dilution, in kJ/mol, positive = endothermic. These values used to ride each species' molar-mass citation, which for three of them said nothing about the enthalpy at all; they are separated here for the same reason the phase-transition tranche was, because an enthalpy of dissolution is a different claim with a different origin from a molar mass, and a heat balance built on it will print it. Fourteen of the seventeen values are consistent with the difference of the standard formation enthalpies commonly tabulated for the aqueous ions and the solid; each row's own `notes` field states that arithmetic explicitly so a reviewer can check it rather than take it on trust. Four of those rows already carried their derivation or a CRC Handbook 97th ed. citation in the species' own provenance line (KOH, NH4Cl, Na2SO4, NH4NO3, plus the NBS/Wagman derivations recorded for ZnSO4 and Pb(NO3)2) and are unchanged in substance. TWO ROWS ARE UNRESOLVED AND ARE NOT SILENTLY FIXED HERE: potassium permanganate's +16.2 kJ/mol reproduces from nothing the reviewer could find and is roughly 27 kJ/mol away from the commonly tabulated heat of solution near +43.6, which is not a sign, unit or hydrate difference; sodium bicarbonate's +16.7 matches neither the formation-enthalpy difference (about +18.7) nor the commonly tabulated figure (about +17.5). Both values are LEFT AS THEY STAND, because changing a number is a separate decision from sourcing one, and both are flagged by name for that decision. The vendored PHREEQC databases were checked as a candidate source and are deliberately NOT cited: Halite's delta_h is 3.84 kJ in wateq4f.dat and 3.7 kJ in minteq.v4.dat against this table's 3.88; Thenardite's is -2.39 kJ and -9.12 kJ in the two files, which disagree with each other; Portlandite's dissolution is written with two protons so its delta_h is the enthalpy of a different reaction entirely; and Chalcanthite is the pentahydrate while this table's copper sulfate is anhydrous. Where a database row IS the better source for a future value it should be cited as the file and reaction line, and none of these seventeen is that case. As with the phase-transition tranche, this is NOT a transcription from a positively identified copy of any single handbook edition, and no edition-level provenance is claimed: the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. and the NBS/Wagman 1982 tables are the intended primary references and every value here is flagged for reviewer confirmation against a positively identified copy before any stronger claim is made. Compiled 2026-09-05

Kerotakis curated electrical-resistivity tranche v1: bulk DC electrical resistivity of the pure solid at 293.15 K (20 C), in ohm.m. THE PROVENANCE LANE OF THIS TRANCHE IS PENDING REVIEW AND THE VALUES ARE RECORDED AS COMMONLY TABULATED. The CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics table 'Electrical Resistivity of Pure Metals' is the intended primary reference and these numbers agree with it to the precision quoted, but this is NOT a transcription from a positively identified copy of any single edition and no edition-level provenance is claimed: every row is flagged for reviewer confirmation against a positively identified copy before any stronger claim is made, exactly as the phase-transition tranche is. The values themselves are physical constants of the pure elements rather than anyone's compilation, and they are quoted only to the three or four figures that a room-temperature handbook column carries; no temperature coefficient, no purity dependence and no cold-worked or alloyed value is claimed, and each row's own `notes` field states what it does not cover. Graphite is the one row that is an order of magnitude rather than a measurement, and its note says so: graphite is strongly anisotropic and its resistivity depends on the grade, so the value here describes a polycrystalline bench rod and nothing finer. Compiled 2026-09-05

Kerotakis household-material assumptions v1: explicit unbranded teaching surrogates for common household substances; ACS middle-school chemistry uses 3% peroxide for yeast catalysis, documents detergent-lowered surface tension, teaches that vegetable oil is less dense than water and does not dissolve in it, demonstrates that detergent helps oil and water mix, and its Colors on the Move activity records detergent driving food colouring rapidly across whole milk; a Journal of Chemical Education baker's-yeast gasometer study measures CO2 evolution, induction, steady production and nutrient depletion, while FAO fermentation material gives the balanced hexose-to-ethanol-and-CO2 pathway; American Society of Baking compressed-yeast technical guidance reports 70% moisture and 30% solids; USDA ERS reports cow's milk as approximately 87% water with the balance milk fat and skim solids; ACS Making Glue and Mississippi State Extension describe vinegar separating milk casein into heavy white curds and liquid whey; USDA FoodData Central's white all-purpose wheat flour entry reports starch as the large majority of its carbohydrate, with protein, moisture, fibre, lipid and ash making up the rest, and its unsweetened apple-juice entry reports roughly 88% water with the sugars dominated by fructose and glucose rather than sucrose and the acidity carried mainly by malic acid; its raw-lemon-juice entry reports roughly 91% water with citric acid as the dominant acid at about 4.7% and ascorbic acid present at about 0.05%; ordinary flat glass is a soda-lime composition of roughly three quarters silica with soda, lime, magnesia and alumina as network modifiers; solid paraffin candle wax and a sheet of office paper are dispensed against room-temperature bulk densities of 0.90 and 0.80 g/mL; USDA FoodData Central's seedless-raisin entry reports roughly 15% water and 79% carbohydrate of which about 59% is sugars, and a dried grape is denser than water at roughly 1.35 g/mL, which is why raisins sink in it

material_recipes.name: doped silicon

roles.boundary: An n-type phosphorus-doped silicon wafer of an ordinary 1 ohm.cm grade. THE VALUE IS ONE POINT IN A RANGE THIS RECIPE DOES NOT PIN DOWN: doped silicon as sold spans about 1e-5 to 1e-1 ohm.m, which end a wafer sits at is set by its dopant concentration - roughly 1e21 to 1e25 atoms per cubic metre - and neither the span nor the reading claims a particular wafer. What changed against the intrinsic-silicon row is the CARRIER DENSITY and nothing else: each dopant atom contributes one mobile electron (phosphorus) or one hole (boron), five to eight orders of magnitude more carriers than the thermal ones, while the lattice, the mobility and the band gap are all essentially as they were. No carrier-density model is computed here and none is claimed - these are two reviewed measurements of two objects, and the sentence between them is the mechanism, not a calculation.

material_recipes.name: thermoplastic sheet

roles.boundary: A moulded high-density polyethylene article. 130 C is the CRYSTALLINE MELT, and it is the threshold this bench uses because it is the one a hot-air gun or a pan of oil actually reaches and the one that lets the object be reshaped. Polyethylene's glass transition is far below room temperature and is not modelled at all; for the amorphous thermoplastics - polystyrene, PVC, acrylic - it is the glass transition rather than a melt that does this job, and this row does not speak for them. Crystallinity, molecular weight and any plasticiser move the melt by tens of kelvin. The 400 C figure is the onset of thermal decomposition and not a boiling point; no degradation product is named, and no viscosity, no rate of flow and no mould-filling behaviour is claimed.
roles.source: Kerotakis curated polymer heat-response tranche v1: the softening (crystalline melt or flow) and decomposition temperatures of the two families of plastic, in K at 101.325 kPa, with a room-temperature specific heat capacity in J/(g.K). THE PROVENANCE LANE OF THIS TRANCHE IS PENDING REVIEW AND THE VALUES ARE RECORDED AS COMMONLY TABULATED. Polymer handbooks and general materials references are the intended primary source, this is NOT a transcription from a positively identified copy of any single edition, no edition-level provenance is claimed, and every row is flagged for reviewer confirmation against a positively identified copy before any stronger claim is made - exactly as the phase-transition and electrical-resistivity tranches are. Polymer transition temperatures are grade-dependent by nature: molecular weight, crystallinity, plasticiser content and degree of cure each move them by tens of kelvin, so these are class figures for a teaching object rather than a specification for any material that could be bought.
